draft.title: Human rights conventions
card: A convention is a written agreement between countries. It sets out standards for how people must be treated, and it is usually made through the United Nations.
Two examples are the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Each covers one area of human rights.
A country chooses to join by signing and then ratifying the convention. Ratifying is the formal step that shows the government agrees to be bound by it.
Australia has ratified both conventions. Its governments can then pass laws that put the standards into practice, such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.
draft.remember: Countries agree to a convention, and the standards in it can shape their own laws.

a.q: What is a human rights convention?
opts: A written agreement between countries on standards
A law made by one country for its own people
A court that punishes countries for abuses
A meeting where leaders talk about rights
a.why: A convention is an agreement that countries make with each other, setting standards for how people are treated. A law made by one country is different, because a convention is made between many countries and a country then uses it to shape its own laws.
a.clue: Think about who makes the agreement.

b.q: Australia ratifies the Convention on the Rights of the Child. What does this show?
opts: The government agrees to be bound by its standards
The convention has become a law in every state
Other countries must now follow Australian law
The United Nations will now run Australian schools
b.why: Ratifying is the formal step by which a government agrees to be bound by a convention. It does not make the convention law by itself. Governments then pass laws that put the standards into practice.
b.clue: Ratifying is a promise by a government, and laws come after.

a.best: A written agreement between countries on standards

b.best: The government agrees to be bound by its standards
